titre: Hastings (1066): Harold's Arrow in the Eye, a Reconstructed Image
accroche: The earliest engravings of the Bayeux Tapestry show a lance in Harold's eye, not an arrow.
contenu_vulgarise:
On the Bayeux Tapestry, one scene shows a warrior with his hand raised to his face, a shaft stuck in his eye, just before a horseman beside him is cut down by a sword. The embroidered caption above reads only: “Here King Harold has been killed.” For two centuries, textbooks and museums have identified this figure as Harold II, King of England, who died on October 14, 1066, at the Battle of Hastings, with an arrow in his eye. The problem: nothing proves the tapestry always showed an arrow at that spot, and no text written in the years after the battle mentions this particular wound.

## What the Earliest Images Actually Show

The Bayeux Tapestry, embroidered in the decades after the Norman conquest for Bishop Odo of Bayeux, William's half-brother, is our most famous image of the scene. But the two oldest known reproductions of this part of the work, the engravings made by Antoine Benoît in 1729 and Bernard de Montfaucon in 1730, show a lance in that hand, not a feathered arrow. Needle holes visible in the linen suggest that an element of the embroidery was removed and then replaced before the tapestry reached its current state. Art historian David Bernstein sums it up in Anglo-Norman Studies: no written account contemporary with the battle mentions an arrow, and the extent of the restorations the work has undergone makes it hard to tell, in its present state, what dates from the eleventh century from what comes from later repairs.

## Silent Texts, Then an Arrow That Arrives in Stages

On the side of the chronicles, the timeline is just as telling. The *Carmen de Hastingae Proelio* (Song of the Battle of Hastings), composed by Guy, Bishop of Amiens, around 1067, a few months after Duke William's coronation, tells of Harold's death by implicating a knight, Hugh of Ponthieu, but mentions no arrow. William of Jumièges, writing around 1070, places the king's death in the early morning fighting, which contradicts the length of the battle given by other sources. William of Poitiers, the duke's chaplain, mentions Harold's death without describing how it happened. The chronicle of Battle Abbey, founded on the very site of the clash, goes further: it states that no one knew, in the crush of combat, who had struck the fatal blow.

The arrow appears in writing only in the 1080s, in the work of the Italian monk Amatus of Montecassino, a witness already judged unreliable by historians: he also credits the Norman army with a hundred thousand fighters, an impossible figure for the period. It then spreads through twelfth-century chronicles, with William of Malmesbury, who adds that it pierced the king's brain, and then with the Norman poet Wace, who in turn repeats the account. Between the battle and these texts, fifteen to sixty years had passed.

## The Shift

The image that circulates today in textbooks owes as much to the restorers of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries as to the embroiderers of the eleventh. It is no accident that this very detail, the most memorable in the whole tapestry, concentrates the bulk of the documented retouching: a confused battle scene, in which several chroniclers admit they do not know who killed the king, has turned over time into a single, sharp image, the one a reader retains at a glance.

repere.texte: The two oldest known engravings of the scene of Harold's death, from 1729 and 1730, show a lance in his eye; the arrow appears only in the tapestry's restored state, and no text written before the 1080s mentions it.
repere.source: Wikipedia, “Bayeux Tapestry” and David Bernstein, “The Blinding of Harold and the Meaning of the Bayeux Tapestry,” Anglo-Norman Studies V, 1983

carte.punch: Before restoration, the Bayeux Tapestry showed a lance in Harold's eye.
carte.idee: The arrow in Harold's eye comes mainly from restorations: the 1729 and 1730 engravings show a lance, needle holes suggest a change, and no text before the 1080s mentions an arrow. Today's textbook image owes as much to the restorers as to the eleventh-century embroiderers.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The poem by Guy, Bishop of Amiens, composed around 1067: the earliest known account of the battle, written with no mention of an arrow.

quiz.question: Why is the image of an arrow in Harold's eye at the Battle of Hastings uncertain?
choix: Because Duke William had every scene depicting the defeated king's death destroyed
Because no copy of the tapestry predates the battle by less than three centuries
Because no account written after the battle mentions an arrow, and the earliest engravings show a lance
Because this scene no longer appears on the tapestry as it is displayed today
quiz.explication: No account written before the 1080s (the Carmen de Hastingae Proelio, William of Jumièges, William of Poitiers) mentions an arrow, and the 1729 and 1730 engravings show a lance: it comes from later restorations and later texts.
